title: Hidden Camera Laws by State 2026: What's Legal, What's Not
excerpt: A state-by-state breakdown of hidden camera laws including recording consent requirements, where cameras are prohibited, penalties for violations, and what changed in 2026.
body:
The Federal Framework

Federal law sets the floor. The Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA) and the Video Voyeurism Prevention Act of 2004 prohibit recording individuals in areas where they have a reasonable expectation of privacy without their consent. Bathrooms, changing rooms, and hotel rooms are universally protected. Penalties include up to one year in federal prison for first-time offenses, two years for repeat violations.

Beyond this federal floor, states can and do provide additional protections. Some states add consent requirements for audio recording, restrict camera placement in rental properties, or create civil liability for violations. Here's what matters state by state.

One-Party vs. All-Party Consent for Audio

Security cameras with audio recording (microphones) are subject to wiretapping and eavesdropping laws that differ significantly by state.

One-party consent states (majority): Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia, Wisconsin, Wyoming. In these states, one person in the conversation must consent to recording — meaning you can record conversations you're part of.

All-party consent states: California, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, Washington. ALL parties must consent to audio recording. Security cameras that pick up conversations in these states may require clear disclosure to all parties.

Key State Laws

California (Strongest Protections)

California Penal Code 632 requires all-party consent for confidential communications. Civil Code 1708.8 prohibits

— using technology to capture images or recordings that couldn't be captured without the technology even from public spaces. Penalties: up to $5,000 per violation plus punitive damages. Hidden cameras in private areas: up to one year in county jail plus a $2,500 fine per offense.

Florida

Security Surveillance Act (§ 810.145) prohibits observation of persons in private places without consent. Misdemeanor for first offense, felony for repeat violations or if a minor is involved. Two-party consent for audio. Distributing recordings from illegal surveillance is a separate felony.

Texas

Invasive Visual Recording law (Penal Code 21.15) prohibits capturing images of private areas without consent. One-party consent for audio. State v. Schmidt established that cameras on your own property filming visible (non-private) areas of a neighbor's property are generally legal.

Illinois

Eavesdropping Act requires all-party consent for audio recording, with criminal penalties up to a Class 4 felony for violations. Illinois courts have found liability for employers recording employees without consent even in common areas. BIPA (Biometric Information Privacy Act) adds additional restrictions on facial recognition technology that would apply to AI-powered security cameras.

New York

Penal Law § 250.45 (Unlawful Surveillance) covers hidden camera placement for sexual gratification, but general privacy torts cover broader misuse. One-party consent for audio. New York City has specific ordinances about cameras in rental units that require landlord disclosure.

Washington

RCW 9.73.030 (Washington Privacy Act) requires all-party consent and applies to any

Courts have broadly interpreted what constitutes private communication. Violation is a class C felony. Washington added specific Airbnb camera disclosure requirements in 2024.

Employer Security Cameras: The Workplace Rules

Employers can generally monitor most workplace areas with security cameras but cannot place cameras in:

  • Bathrooms or changing rooms (illegal in all 50 states)
  • Locations specifically to monitor union organizing activity (federal labor law violation)
  • Areas where employees have a stated expectation of privacy

Notice requirements vary: many states require employers to notify employees of camera monitoring. California, Connecticut, Delaware, and New York have the most explicit notification requirements.

Landlord-Tenant Rules for Security Cameras

Landlords generally cannot place cameras inside tenant living spaces. In common areas (hallways, lobbies, parking lots):

  • Most states allow cameras in common areas with proper disclosure in the lease
  • California requires written lease disclosure
  • New York City Local Law 110 (2024) requires landlords to disclose all camera locations to tenants
  • Airbnb and VRBO's 2026 policies now ban all indoor cameras in rental properties regardless of state law, setting a stricter standard than most state laws

Penalties Summary by Violation Type

Placing a camera in a bathroom or private area: Federal: up to 1 year prison + fines. State: varies from misdemeanor to Class A felony depending on intent and whether minors are involved.

Recording audio without consent in all-party states: California: up to $5,000 civil penalty per violation plus punitive damages, criminal penalties up to 1 year. Illinois: Class 4 felony (1-3 years).

Distributing or sharing illegal recordings: Federal and state charges. Federal: up to 5 years for distribution. Most states add felony-level distribution charges.

Legitimate Uses That Are Legal in All States

Cameras are legal to install in: your own home's public-facing areas (doorbell, driveway, yard visible from the street), business common areas with disclosure, professional offices and storefronts with posted notice, your own vehicle interior and exterior, and any area where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy.

When in doubt: disclose. A visible camera with posted notice ("Security cameras in use") reduces legal exposure dramatically and deters crime more effectively than hidden cameras in most legal use cases.
